title: OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
shortTitle: OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
summary: The Security Account Manager sub-technique targets the local account database on a Windows host, which stores password hashes for accounts that exist only on that machine, such as the built-in administrator and locally created users. The data sits in a registry hive that Windows locks while running, so the adversary either reads it from memory or copies the hive offline, commonly by saving the SAM hive together with the SYSTEM hive because the second holds the key material needed to interpret the first. SYSTEM level access is required, and the recovered hashes cover local accounts only, yet they still support lateral movement wherever the same local password is reused. Detection focuses on registry hive save operations, unusual creation of hive sized files, and command lines that name the SAM or SYSTEM keys. Approved backup and forensic tooling performs the same steps, so provenance and timing carry the weight.

beginner.definition: The SAM is a Windows database that stores local account passwords as hashes. This sub-technique means copying that database to steal the hashes. It differs from the parent because the source is a registry hive. That hive holds local accounts, not process memory or a domain database.
beginner.whyItMatters: Local administrator passwords are often reused across many computers. One copied database can therefore unlock several machines. The copied file can be taken away and examined without touching the host again. Built-in commands can export the hive, so the action may look routine. Watching registry exports helps you catch the theft early.
howItWorks: Windows keeps local account details in a registry hive called the SAM.
The hive is locked while the system runs, so a simple file copy usually fails.
The attacker saves the SAM and SYSTEM hives into an ordinary folder instead.
Sometimes memory is read to obtain the same data without touching those files.
The saved files are moved to another machine for offline processing.
Recovered hashes are reused for logon or cracked later to reveal passwords.
beginner.example: Think of a small office with one filing cabinet holding local staff records. Each branch uses the same simple lock and the same key. A visitor with building access photographs every page in one cabinet and leaves the room tidy. Weeks later, those copies open the cabinets in other branches. The SAM is that local filing cabinet, and the photographs are the stolen hashes.
takeaways: SAM hashes cover local accounts, so password reuse spreads the damage.
Registry hive save operations are the main artefact to watch for.
Backup tools export hives too, so confirm who ran the export and why.

objectives: Explain what the Windows Security Account Manager database contains.
Describe why the hive must be copied offline rather than read directly.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the credential dumping parent.
Identify command and file artefacts produced by saving a registry hive.
Explain how local account password reuse increases the impact of a dump.
